title: The cost of starting on Monday.
dek: There are 9 Mondays left in 2026. Every one that gets promised something costs about four days, and a little of your trust in your own word.
whyThisIdea: Today is 31 October, with 9 Mondays left in the year and the “I will start in January” season about to begin. It is also the sentence the last two posts kept running into, so this picks up idea #13 from the backlog and follows straight on from them.

entry.title: The cost of starting on Monday.
entry.titleHtml: The cost of starting on Monday.
entry.dek: There are 9 Mondays left in 2026. Every one that gets promised something costs about four days, and a little of your trust in your own word.
body: “Monday is not a plan. It is a place to put one.”

Have you ever asked yourself how many Mondays you have promised something to? Not done something on, just promised. I tried to count mine and I gave up, which is already an answer. Today is the last day of October, and there are exactly 9 Mondays left in 2026, from the 2nd of November to the 28th of December. So the question is: why does a plan feel safer when it starts on a Monday, and what does that safety actually cost? Let’s start from the beginning.

The sentence is “I will start on Monday”, and if you read this blog you have already met it twice. In the Atomic Habits review I wrote about the voice that says “I will start from Monday” and how it keeps you on the outside of a habit. Two days ago, in the article about the maths, it came back as the line that follows two missed days in a row. Two appearances in a blog this young is a lot for a sentence I never really looked at, so today I want to take it apart.

Firstly, let’s split it in two, the way I like to do with a title. “I will start” is the decision. “On Monday” is the delay. The trick is that the first half gives you almost the whole good feeling of starting - you picked the thing, you said it out loud, maybe you even told someone. And then the second half quietly removes the only part that costs anything. <u>Saying “I will start on Monday” feels like a beginning, but it is a way to get the reward of a decision without paying for it.</u> By the time Monday comes, the good feeling is already spent, and what is left is just the work.

Secondly, let’s put a number on the delay, because it is bigger than it looks. If you decide on a Tuesday, waiting for Monday costs you six days. If you decide on a Sunday, one. If you decide on a Monday and still say “next Monday” (I have done this), seven. Take the average over the seven days of the week and it comes to four days lost every single time. That is small once. But a year has 52 Mondays, and the sentence does not get used once - it gets used every time a week goes badly, which is exactly when you need it least.

Now the bigger version, which is the one that is waiting for all of us right now. At the end of October, the most tempting Monday is not next week, it is January. “I will start in the new year.” Except the 1st of January 2027 is a Friday, so the new year, for anyone who wants a clean start, really means Monday the 4th of January.
From today, the 31st of October, to the 4th of January: 65 days
From Monday the 2nd of November to the 4th of January: 63 days, and 9 Mondays that go by unused
And if I take the same formula from the article two days ago and pretend I showed up on every one of those days, 1.0163 = 1.87. Nobody would notice 1.87 on me. But that is not the point of the 63 days, the point is that on the 4th of January I would be on day 64 instead of day 1.

There is also a cost that does not fit in a formula. Every Monday that was promised something and did not get it teaches you a small lesson: that your own promises are negotiable. Once is nothing. But after a few of them, the sentence “I will start on Monday” stops being a plan even to you - you hear yourself say it and part of you already knows it will not happen. I think this is the real price. Not the days, but the trust you have in your own word, spent four days at a time.

Thirdly, and this is where I have to be fair to Monday. There is real research saying that fresh starts work. In 2014, Hengchen Dai, Katherine Milkman and Jason Riis published a study they called “The Fresh Start Effect”, and they found that people are more likely to go after their goals right after a landmark in time - the start of a week, of a month, of a year, a birthday. A new date draws a line between the old you and the new you, and that line helps. So Monday is not useless. The problem is not the landmark, it is the empty space in front of it. A fresh start is worth something if you arrive at it already moving, and almost nothing if you are only arriving at it to begin.

So here is what I am going to do, because an article like this is worthless if it ends only in agreement. Today is a Saturday, which is the worst possible day to start anything according to my own instincts. That is exactly why I will start today, with the smallest version of the thing - ten minutes, nothing more - and let Monday be the third day instead of the first. If the fresh start effect is real, it should work even better on someone who already has two days behind him. And if I miss one, the rule from last time still stands: never miss twice.

For today, that will be all. My personal opinion? I think “start now” is right, but I also think it is a bit too easy to say, and I do not fully trust advice that sounds that clean. Sometimes waiting really is the correct choice - if you need running shoes, Monday is a reasonable day to have bought them by, and nobody should feel guilty for planning. And I have to admit something: while writing this, on a Saturday, part of me was already thinking that Monday would be a nicer day to start. So I am not above the sentence. What I believe is smaller: Monday can be the day you continue, it just should not be the day you begin.
In the end, I hope you enjoyed this article and I will leave you with the line that started all of this. Peace!
“Monday is not a plan. It is a place to put one.”
